items.headline: Nvidia staff press the board to bring Huang back, hours before earnings
items.summary: Senior Nvidia employees wrote to the board that failing to reinstate Jensen Huang could cost the company "irreplaceable talent," per the WSJ via @KobeissiLetter, and some discussed a campus demonstration. Nvidia also set up a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee with outside experts. Commerce and the DOJ said Nvidia handed over records in May 2025 and the probe targets Megaspeed, @ren_stocks noted. Earnings are tonight; @jimcramer expects a big gross-margin cut.
items.short: Employees push for Huang's return; a new compliance committee; earnings tonight.

items.headline: Isomorphic Labs raises $5B to redesign drug discovery with AI
items.summary: Demis Hassabis announced $5 billion in funding for Isomorphic Labs, the Alphabet spinout working to cut the time and cost of finding new medicines by designing drugs from first principles with AI. "Gradually, then all at once," he wrote.

items.headline: Apple turns to Samsung and SK Hynix for long-term memory supply
items.summary: Apple signed long-term supply agreements with Samsung and SK Hynix, Korea's Maeil Business Newspaper reported via @jukan05, with similar deals believed signed with Kioxia. @aleabitoreddit reads it as Apple giving up on cheap Chinese DRAM: contracts start in H1 2027 and run 4-5 years, which adds demand visibility for memory makers.
items.short: Multi-year memory deals add demand visibility.

items.author: Serenity
items.text:
Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary. 

Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later. 

I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc. 

The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem. 

But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming). 

- It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far. 

- Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations)

- Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes.

On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN  seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties. 

What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains.

- Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity.  
- MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers
- ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere. 

If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%. 

And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply... 

I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping. 

Another rant is: 

-I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes

Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last. 

If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E. 

- Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO. 

We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage. 

- Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have.

If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued.  

TLDR:
- I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios. 

Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued. 

- This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet). 

- We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere.  

The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on. 

Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

- Fully autonomous vulnerability exploitation is now happening

- Adversaries transitioned beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks

- AI is collapsing the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation

- Google believes cybersecurity defense must become autonomous too

by combining Gemini and other frontier models for reasoning + smaller models for continuous scanning.

I’d actually argue beneficiaries of this arms race are AI compute and infra providers, regardless of the cybersecurity winners.

Since cybersecurity will become a source of persistent inference consumption.

$AMZN CEO Andy Jassy's also quoted estimates earlier that 20% of AI tokens could go toward cybersecurity.

Believe it or not, the rise of persistent cyberattacks from hostile state actors… is a structural driver for long term compute demand.

items.author: Fireside Alpha
items.text:
Marc Andreessen says both AI utopians and doomers will be disappointed because new technologies can be frozen in their tracks, as nuclear power was

“My line has been both utopians and the doomers are gonna be disappointed. Specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact.”

“And I think the reason for that is basically as follows: the world is a very complicated and messy place. And just because there’s a new technology, and just because it looks like there’s obvious ways to deploy it and things that should happen, does not mean that any of that actually happens.”

“And in fact, there are historical precedents for new technologies that have simply been frozen in their tracks. And the big one in our lifetimes has been civilian nuclear power, which at one point was the panacea for US energy, global energy growth.”

“And by the way, it was zero-emission, carbon-free technology that in retrospect would have been tremendously beneficial, even from the environmental standpoint. And it was basically killed. By the way, the remnants of it are being killed both in the US and Europe right now.”

“So these things don’t have to get deployed. Sometimes they’re simply stopped.”

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a person is drinking beer, they must be over 21.
items.explanation: Drinking beer could hide something that breaks the rule; Age 17 breaks it if the other side turns out to be Drinking beer. Age 25 can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Drinking soda isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it. Most people get this version right and the letters-and-numbers version wrong, though the logic is identical.

across.clue: A band that goes over the shoulder and supports a garment or bag
A craftsman who works with stone or brick
A yearning for something or to do something

down.clue: Wander from a direct course or at random
Come into existence; take on form or shape
A priest who is a member of a cathedral chapter
A writing implement with a point from which ink flows
